newsitem.title: USA: Media/telecom issuers ready exchangeable pfd deals.
newsitem.headline: Media/telecom issuers ready exchangeable pfd deals.

text.p: U.S. media and telecommunications companies plan to raise over $500 million through private offerings of leveraged preferred stock exchangeable for junk bonds over the next few weeks, according to market sources.
Analysts noted the deals will help the companies finance an ongoing acquisition boom in the industry that began following last year's telecommunications reform legislation.

Chancellor Radio Broadcasting of Dallas, Texas; American Radio Systems Corp of Boston, Mass.; Pegasus Communications Corp, a Radnor, Penn.-based media and communications company; and Nextlink Communications, a Bellevue, Wash.-based competitive local exchange carrier, plan to price new deals. (See table below for details.)
Sinclair Broadcating Group Inc and Granite Broadcasting are also said to be considering offerings.

Market experts said the recent popularity of exchangeable preferred stock is the result of a combination of factors including the unique financing needs of the media and telecommunications industry as well as the strength of the high-yield market.
Issuing preferred stock allows these growing companies, which are already heavily leveraged, to borrow more funds without increasing their debt ratios on paper.
Analysts said banks which typically lend to this industry restrict their debt-to-cash flow ratio to 6:1 or 7:1. But banks do not consider preferred stock to be debt, they noted.

"(Preferred stock) gives the companies financial flexibility to leverage themselves eight to nine times (cash flow) without getting into trouble with banks," said one analyst who declined to be named.

Companies in similar situations would typically look to the stock market for funds; but market experts said the equity valuations of broadcasters are currently depressed, making that a very expensive option.
Analysts said the exchangeable structure gives broadcasters the ability to receive the tax advantages of debt financing when and if they are able to increase their cash flows.

Les Levi, media and telecom high-yield analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, noted: "If a company finds that it is generating substantial income, it is to its advantage to exchange preferred into a subordinate note, so that dividend payments become tax-deductible interest expenses."
In fact, the securities are being marketed primarily to high-yield investors who will benefit if the securities are exchanged for bonds, which have greater credit protection.
From an investor's point of view, however, the securities also carry considerable risk.
Unlike most preferred stock, which pays dividends in cash, most of these securities pay in-kind (PIK), meaning investors receive their dividend payments in the form of additional securities.
As with zero coupon bonds, the securities only start to pay cash after a number of years, presumably once the issuer has increased its cash flow through acquisitions.
Unlike zero coupon bonds, however, preferred stocks rank below bonds in the capital structure and offer investors little protection in the event of a bankruptcy.
"If the company fails to make a dividend payment, a preferred stockholder has very little remedy," said one analyst.
To compensate investors for the extra risk, the securities are likely to offer sizable yields of over 13 percent, which are attractive even by junk market standards.

"These are vehicles which allow high growth companies to get additional leverage," said G. Robert Berzins, media and communications high-yield analyst at Lehman Brothers Inc. "From an investor's standpoint, they are designed for more aggressive players."

Dean Kartsonas, media and telecommunications analyst at Federated Investors, added: "We are not afraid of the structure, but because you are at the bottom of the capital structure, it makes being comfortable with the company's credit profile all the more important."
He further pointed out: "Spreads have gotten so tight in the junk market. This potentially gives you some extra juice."
